l: book of Baruch, Baruch, Baruch / Chapter 1
s: The book is written in Babylon and read aloud to Jechonias and the exiles, who respond with weeping, fasting, and prayer. It is then sent to Jerusalem with money, to be read in the house of the Lord on feast days and days of solemn assembly as a confession of sin.

l: Babylon, Baruch, Baruch / Chapter 1
s: Babylon is where Baruch wrote and read the book and where the exiles, including Jechonias, live by the river Sud. Nabuchodonosor, its king, carried Jechonias, the princes, the mighty men, and the people of the land there from Jerusalem.

l: Jerusalem, Baruch, Baruch / Chapter 1
s: Jerusalem was taken and burned by the Chaldeans at the time Baruch wrote his book. The exiles send money there to Joakim the high priest and the priests, and the book is to be read in the house of the Lord.

l: Jechonias, Baruch, Baruch / Chapter 1
s: Jechonias, son of Joakim king of Judah, is present in Babylon when Baruch reads the book in his hearing. He had earlier been carried away to Babylon by Nabuchodonosor along with the princes, captives, and mighty men.

l: Nabuchodonosor, Baruch, Baruch / Chapter 1
s: Nabuchodonosor, king of Babylon, had carried Jechonias, the princes, the mighty men, and the people of the land from Jerusalem to Babylon. The exiles ask that prayers be offered for his life and that of his son Baltasar, and say they will live under their shadow and serve them many days.

l: God, Baruch, Baruch / Chapter 1
s: The Lord is the one to whom righteousness belongs, while his wrath and indignation have not turned from the people. He brought the fathers out of Egypt, declared a curse through Moses, and sent prophets whose voice the people did not heed.

l: exiles at Babylon, Baruch, Baruch / Chapter 1
s: The exiles hear the book, then weep, fast, and pray before the Lord. They collect money according to each one's ability, send it to Jerusalem, and ask for prayer for themselves, confessing that they have sinned against the Lord.

l: collection of money, Baruch, Baruch / Chapter 1
s: The exiles gathered money according to every man's ability and sent it to Joakim the high priest and the priests in Jerusalem. It was meant to buy burnt offerings, sin offerings, and incense and to prepare an oblation for the altar of the Lord, and was sent at the time the vessels of the house of the Lord were returned to Judah.

l: Israel's sin and confession, Baruch, Baruch / Chapter 1
s: The people are to confess that righteousness belongs to the Lord and confusion of face to Judah, Jerusalem, and their kings, princes, priests, prophets, and fathers. They admit disobedience since the exodus from Egypt, ignoring the prophets and following their own wicked hearts to serve strange gods, which brought the plagues and the curse upon them.

l: Baruch, Baruch, Chapter 2
s: In this chapter the speaker, praying on behalf of the people, confesses that the Lord has fulfilled the word he pronounced against Israel, its judges, kings, princes, and the men of Israel and Judah, bringing great plagues including cannibalism of sons and daughters, as written in the law of Moses. The people admit they sinned by not listening to the Lord's voice, and they ask him to turn away his wrath, hear their prayer, and deliver them for his own sake, appealing not to the righteousness of their fathers and kings but to his mercy. They recall the prophets' command to serve the king of Babylon and remain in the land, and acknowledge that refusing led to desolation, the silencing of the voices of mirth and the bridegroom and bride, and the casting out of the bones of their kings and fathers. The chapter closes by recalling the Lord's word through Moses that the stiff-necked people would be reduced to a small number among the nations, yet in captivity would take it to heart, repent, and be brought back to the land promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob under an everlasting covenant.

l: God, Baruch, Chapter 2
s: The Lord is described as righteous in all his works, having fulfilled the word he pronounced through the law of Moses and the prophets by bringing plagues and scattering on the people. The people appeal to him for mercy, recalling that he brought Israel out of Egypt with a mighty hand and made himself a name. He is recalled as promising through Moses to give the people a heart and ears to hear, to bring them back to the land, and to make an everlasting covenant so that he is their God and they are his people.

l: Israel, Baruch, Chapter 2
s: Israel, together with its judges, kings, princes, and the men of Israel and Judah, is confessed to have sinned and been ungodly, and now is only a few left among the nations. The people plead for deliverance because they are called by the Lord's name, not because of the righteousness of their fathers and kings. They are recalled as a stiff-necked people who will repent in captivity and be restored, never again to be removed from their land.

l: Babylon, Baruch, Chapter 2
s: The king of Babylon is the one whom the prophets, speaking for the Lord, told the people to serve while remaining in the land. The people confess they refused to listen and serve him, and so the Lord's warning of desolation came true.

l: sin and plagues, Baruch, Chapter 2
s: The great plagues, such as never happened before under heaven and as occurred in Jerusalem, include eating the flesh of one's own son and daughter, as written in the law of Moses. The people state that all these plagues have come as the Lord pronounced, and that their kings and fathers died in great miseries by famine, sword, and pestilence.

l: the captivity and scattering, Baruch, Chapter 2
s: The Lord has scattered the people among the surrounding nations, subjecting them to the kingdoms around them as a reproach and desolation, leaving only a few. The people ask for favor in the sight of their captors. The Lord's word through Moses foretells that in captivity they will take it to heart, know the Lord, praise him, and return from their wicked deeds.

l: the land promised to the fathers, Baruch, Chapter 2
s: The land was given to the people's fathers, and the prophets told the people to remain in it while serving the king of Babylon. Disobedience would make the cities of Judah and the region near Jerusalem desolate without inhabitant, silencing the voices of mirth, gladness, bridegroom, and bride. The Lord promises to bring them again into the land promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, where they will rule, increase, and never again be removed.

l: sin and disobedience, Baruch, Chapter 2
s: The people confess that they sinned against the Lord by not listening to his voice, not turning from the thoughts of their wicked hearts, and not walking in his commandments. They say they have been ungodly and done wrong in all his ordinances, and that they refused to serve the king of Babylon despite the prophets. Moses is recalled as describing them as stiff-necked, though they will eventually turn from their stiff neck and wicked deeds.

l: Baruch, Baruch, Chapter 3
s: In Chapter 3, the afflicted people of Israel cry out to the Lord Almighty, the God of Israel, confessing that they and their fathers have sinned and asking for mercy rather than remembered iniquity. They lament that they are in captivity among enemies, a reproach and a curse, because they forsook the fountain of wisdom. Israel is urged to learn where wisdom, strength, understanding, life and peace are found. The text says the rulers, silver-hoarders, giants, and foreign peoples such as the sons of Agar and the merchants of Merran and Teman never found wisdom's way and perished in their foolishness. Only God, who knows all things, found wisdom; he gave it to Jacob and Israel, and afterward she appeared on earth and lived with men.

l: Israel, Baruch, Chapter 3
s: Israel prays in anguish, confessing that it and its fathers sinned and are now scattered in an enemy land, grown old in a strange country, defiled with the dead and counted with those in Hades. It is told it forsook the fountain of wisdom, is exhorted to hear the commandments of life, and is finally said to be the one to whom God gave the way of knowledge.

l: wisdom, Baruch, Chapter 3
s: Wisdom is called the fountain Israel forsook; walking in God's way would have meant peace forever. No one has found her place or treasuries: not the princes, hoarders of silver, giants, nor the sons of Agar and merchants of Merran and Teman. No one can go up to heaven or across the sea to fetch her. Only God knows her, found her with his understanding, and gave her to Jacob and Israel, after which she appeared on earth and lived with men.

l: captivity of Israel's children, Baruch, Chapter 3
s: Captivity is the condition in which the people now live, scattered by God in their enemies' land as a reproach and a curse and subject to penalty for their fathers' iniquities. In it they nonetheless promise to praise the Lord and call on his name, having called to mind their fathers' sins.

l: sin and plagues, Baruch, Chapter 3
s: The people confess that they have sinned before God and that their fathers did not listen to his voice, departing from him. Because of this, plagues cling to them, and they are subject to penalty according to their fathers' iniquities; they ask that those iniquities not be remembered.

l: Baruch, Baruch, Chapter 4
s: Chapter 4 opens by declaring the book of God's commandments to be the enduring law, giving life to those who hold it and death to those who leave it. It urges Jacob and Israel to take hold of it and not give their glory to another. Personified Jerusalem, speaking as a desolate widow, explains that her children were delivered to a shameless, foreign-tongued nation because they provoked God with sacrifices to demons and abandoned his law. She then urges the children to take courage, cry to God, and seek him ten times more, trusting that he will bring them salvation and joy. The chapter ends by promising doom for the cities that afflicted and enslaved Israel's children, and by calling Jerusalem to look east and see her sons returning, gathered from east to west at the word of the Holy One.

l: God, Baruch, Chapter 4
s: God is the one who made Israel, was provoked to wrath by their sacrifices to demons, and delivered them to their adversaries, though not to destroy them. He is called the Everlasting and the Holy One, and is promised to deliver the people, bring them everlasting joy, punish the cities that afflicted them, and gather Jerusalem's sons at his word.

l: Jerusalem, Baruch, Chapter 4
s: Jerusalem speaks as a desolate widow who nursed her children, sent them away weeping, and now puts on sackcloth and cries to the Everlasting. She admits she cannot help them herself but trusts God to save them. She is told to take courage because God, who called her by name, will comfort her, and to look east to see her sons returning.

l: Israel, Baruch, Chapter 4
s: Israel, addressed also as Jacob and as God's people, is told to take hold of the law and walk toward its light. They were handed to their adversaries not for destruction but because they provoked God with sacrifices to demons and forgot him. They are urged to suffer patiently, return and seek God ten times more, and expect to see their enemy destroyed.

l: book of God's commandments, Baruch, Chapter 4
s: It is described as the law that endures forever. Those who hold it fast will live, and those who leave it will die. Israel's children were punished because they turned from the law and did not walk in God's commandments or discipline.

l: foreign nation (Israel's captors), Baruch, Chapter 4
s: God brought this nation from afar against Israel. It is described as shameless, speaking a strange language, and showing no respect for old men or pity for children. It carried off the widow's sons and daughters, and the chapter foretells that its enemy-persecutors will be destroyed and trodden upon, and that the city which received Israel's sons will be grieved in desolation, burned by fire, and inhabited by demons.

l: captivity of Israel's children, Baruch, Chapter 4
s: Jerusalem's sons and daughters were carried off like a flock taken by enemies and traveled rough roads, a captivity brought on by God because of their sins. Jerusalem called on those near Zion to remember it and mourned the sending away of her children with weeping.

l: salvation and return of Israel, Baruch, Chapter 4
s: The chapter promises that God will deliver the people from their enemies' hand and give them back to Jerusalem with joy and gladness forever. Those near Zion will shortly see their salvation with great glory, and the chapter closes with the sons coming gathered from east to west, rejoicing in God's glory.

l: Baruch, Baruch, Chapter 5
s: Chapter 5 addresses Jerusalem, telling her to remove her mourning and affliction and put on the beauty of God's glory, the robe of righteousness, and a diadem. God will show her splendor everywhere under heaven and will call her by the name "Righteous Peace, Godly Glory". Jerusalem is told to stand on the height and see her children gathered from west to east at the word of the Holy One, rejoicing that God remembered them. Whereas they left on foot as captives of their enemies, God now brings them back carried on high on a royal throne. God has ordered mountains and hills made low and valleys filled so Israel may walk safely, and the woods and sweet smelling trees shade Israel, as God leads Israel with joy in the light of his glory, with mercy and righteousness.

l: Jerusalem, Baruch, Chapter 5
s: Jerusalem is commanded to take off her garment of mourning and affliction and put on the beauty of God's glory, the robe of righteousness, and a diadem of the glory of the Everlasting. She is told her splendor will be shown everywhere under heaven and that God will call her "Righteous Peace, Godly Glory" forever. She is also told to arise, stand on the height, and look east to see her children gathered.

l: God, Baruch, Chapter 5
s: God will show Jerusalem's splendor under heaven, give her a lasting name, and remember her scattered children. He brings the children back carried on high on a royal throne, has appointed the mountains and hills to be made low and the valleys filled so Israel can go safely, and commands the woods and sweet smelling trees to shade Israel. He will lead Israel with joy in the light of his glory, with mercy and righteousness that come from him.

l: Israel, Baruch, Chapter 5
s: Israel is to go safely in the glory of God along a level ground made by the lowering of mountains and hills and the filling of valleys. The woods and every sweet smelling tree have shaded Israel at God's command. God will lead Israel with joy in the light of his glory, with mercy and righteousness.

l: children (Jerusalem's children), Baruch, Chapter 5
s: Jerusalem's children are seen gathered from the going down of the sun to its rising at the word of the Holy One, rejoicing that God has remembered them. They had gone from Jerusalem on foot, led away by their enemies, but God now brings them back carried on high with glory on a royal throne.

l: glory of God, Baruch, Chapter 5
s: The glory of God is the beauty Jerusalem is told to put on forever, and the light in which God will lead Israel with joy. Israel is to go safely in it, and Jerusalem's name will include "Godly Glory". The children are brought back with glory, and a diadem of the glory of the Everlasting is set on Jerusalem's head.

l: Baruch, Baruch, The Letter of Jeremiah
s: The Letter of Jeremiah is a letter Jeremy sent to those about to be led captive to Babylon by Nabuchodonosor, king of the Babylonians, as God commanded. He tells them the captivity is punishment for their sins, that it will last seven generations, and that God will afterward bring them out peacefully. He warns them not to fear or imitate the gods of silver, gold, and wood they will see carried on shoulders in Babylon. He mocks these idols at length: they cannot speak, see, save themselves from rust, thieves, war, or fire, or help the weak, while their priests steal from them and sell their offerings. He contrasts them with the sun, moon, stars, lightning, wind, clouds, and fire, which obey God, and concludes that the just man without idols is better because he will be far from reproach.

l: Jeremy, Baruch, The Letter of Jeremiah
s: Jeremy sends a letter to those about to be led captive into Babylon, delivering the message God commanded him to give. In it he tells them why they are being taken, how long they will stay, and warns them repeatedly not to fear the Babylonian idols.

l: captives (Jeremy's addressees), Baruch, The Letter of Jeremiah
s: The captives are told they will be led to Babylon by Nabuchodonosor because of their sins, and will remain there for seven generations before God brings them out peacefully. They are warned not to become like the foreigners, not to fear the idols when they see crowds worshiping them, and to say in their hearts, "O Lord, we must worship you."

l: Babylon, Baruch, The Letter of Jeremiah
s: Babylon is the place of the captives' exile, where they will stay many years, even seven generations. It is where they will see idols of silver, gold, and wood carried on shoulders, worshiped by multitudes, and dishonored even by the Chaldeans themselves.

l: God, Baruch, The Letter of Jeremiah
s: God commanded Jeremy's message, and his angel is said to be with the captives, while he himself cares for their souls. He promises to bring them out of Babylon peacefully, and he commands the clouds, sun, moon, stars, wind, and fire, which obey him, unlike the idols.

l: Babylonian idols, Baruch, The Letter of Jeremiah
s: The idols are described as gods of wood overlaid with silver and gold, made by carpenters and goldsmiths, and unable to speak, see, feel, or move without being carried. They cannot save themselves from rust, dust, thieves, war, plague, or fire, cannot bless or curse kings, give rain, or help the widow and the weak. They are compared to scarecrows, beams, and dead bodies, and are declared to be no gods, so the captives should not fear them.

l: priests (of Babylonian idols), Baruch, The Letter of Jeremiah
s: The priests take gold and silver from the idols to spend on themselves, give some to prostitutes, and sell the sacrifices offered to them. Their wives salt away part of the offerings and give none to the poor, and the priests also strip the idols' garments to clothe their own wives and children. They lock their temples against robbers and sit with torn clothes and shaven heads, and when war, plague, or fire comes they plan to hide or flee, leaving the idols to burn.

l: idolatry (futility of idol worship), Baruch, The Letter of Jeremiah
s: The letter argues that idol worship is futile because the idols are lifeless human creations that cannot act, judge, help, or defend themselves, and it repeatedly says "Therefore don't fear them." Those who serve them will be confounded, and the text concludes that the just man who has no idols is better, for he will be far from reproach.

l: The Book of Joel, The Book of Joel, The Book of Joel / Chapter 1
s: Chapter 1 of the Book of Joel opens with the LORD's word coming to Joel, the son of Pethuel, who calls the elders and all inhabitants of the land to hear of a calamity unprecedented in their days and to pass the account to future generations. Successive waves of locusts, grasshoppers and caterpillars, described as a strong, countless nation with lion's teeth, have stripped the vines, fig trees, grain and fields. As a result drunkards lose their wine, farmers and vineyard keepers wail, joy withers, and the meal and drink offerings are cut off from the LORD's house, so the priests mourn. Joel summons the priests and ministers to put on sackcloth, sanctify a fast, call a solemn assembly, and cry to the LORD, warning that the day of the LORD is at hand as destruction from the Almighty. The chapter ends with Joel's own cry to the LORD, as fire devours the wilderness pastures, the water brooks dry up, and the animals groan and pant.

l: LORD, The Book of Joel, The Book of Joel / Chapter 1
s: The LORD's word comes to Joel, and the offerings are cut off from the LORD's house. The people are told to cry to him, and the day of the LORD is said to come as destruction from the Almighty. Joel cries to the LORD as fire devours the pastures and the animals of the field pant to him.

l: inhabitants of the land, The Book of Joel, The Book of Joel / Chapter 1
s: The elders and all inhabitants of the land are called to hear and to tell their children about an unprecedented calamity. They are later told to gather at the LORD's house for a solemn assembly and cry to the LORD. They suffer the loss of food, wine and joy.

l: locust plague, The Book of Joel, The Book of Joel / Chapter 1
s: Successive swarms (the swarming locust, great locust, grasshopper and caterpillar) eat whatever the previous one left. The invader is described as a strong nation without number with the teeth of a lion and the fangs of a lioness. It lays waste the vine and fig tree, stripping the bark and leaving branches white.

l: priests, The Book of Joel, The Book of Joel / Chapter 1
s: The priests, the LORD's ministers, mourn because the meal offering and drink offering are cut off from the LORD's house. They are commanded to put on sackcloth, wail, and lie all night in sackcloth as ministers of the altar and of God.

l: land of Joel's people, The Book of Joel, The Book of Joel / Chapter 1
s: The land is laid waste and mourns as grain is destroyed, new wine dries up and oil languishes. A nation has come up on it, and fire has devoured the wilderness pastures. Its water brooks are dried up, and its livestock and flocks are desolate.

l: crops and trees, The Book of Joel, The Book of Joel / Chapter 1
s: The vine, fig tree, pomegranate, palm, apple and all the trees of the field wither, and the wheat, barley and harvest perish. Seeds rot under clods, granaries are desolate and barns broken down. Joy withers away from the sons of men with them.

l: day of the LORD, The Book of Joel, The Book of Joel / Chapter 1
s: Joel cries 'Alas for the day!' and declares that the day of the LORD is at hand. It will come as destruction from the Almighty.

l: fast and solemn assembly, The Book of Joel, The Book of Joel / Chapter 1
s: Joel commands that a fast be sanctified and a solemn assembly called. The elders and all inhabitants of the land are to gather at the LORD's house and cry to the LORD.

l: The Book of Joel, The Book of Joel, Chapter 2
s: Chapter 2 opens with a trumpet alarm in Zion warning that the day of the LORD is near, describing a vast, unstoppable army that brings darkness, devouring fire, and cosmic shaking. The LORD, however, calls his people to return to him with all their heart, fasting, weeping, and mourning, tearing their hearts rather than their garments, because he is gracious, merciful, and slow to anger. The people, priests, elders, and children are summoned to a solemn assembly, and the priests plead for the LORD to spare his people. The LORD then becomes jealous for his land, pities his people, removes the northern army, and promises grain, new wine, oil, rain, and restoration of the years the locusts ate. He further promises to pour out his Spirit on all flesh, show wonders before the great and terrible day of the LORD, and save whoever calls on his name.

l: LORD, The Book of Joel, Chapter 2
s: The LORD thunders before his army, then calls his people to return to him with all their heart. After the priests plead, he becomes jealous for his land and pities his people, promising grain, wine, oil, and rain, removing the northern army, and restoring the years the locusts ate. He also promises to pour out his Spirit on all flesh and to save those who call on his name.

l: Zion, The Book of Joel, Chapter 2
s: Zion is where the trumpet is blown to sound the alarm and later to sanctify a fast and call a solemn assembly. Its children are told to be glad and rejoice in the LORD, and Mount Zion and Jerusalem are named as places where there will be those who escape.

l: day of the LORD, The Book of Joel, Chapter 2
s: The day of the LORD is described as close at hand, a day of darkness, gloominess, clouds and thick darkness, great and very awesome, such that no one can endure it. The earth quakes, the heavens tremble, and the sun, moon, and stars are darkened. Later it is called the great and terrible day, preceded by the sun turning to darkness and the moon to blood.

l: invading army (the LORD's army), The Book of Joel, Chapter 2
s: The army is described as a great and strong people unlike any before, looking like horses, running like warriors, marching in unbroken ranks, with fire before and behind them, climbing walls and entering houses like thieves. It is the LORD's army before which he thunders, and the land is like Eden before it and a desolate wilderness behind. The LORD promises to remove the northern army into a barren land, driving it into the eastern and western seas, and its stench will rise.

l: people of Israel (the LORD's people), The Book of Joel, Chapter 2
s: The people are told to tremble, gather, and assemble, from elders to nursing children and newlyweds, and the priests plead that they not become a reproach among the nations. The LORD pities them, promises they will be satisfied and never again be disappointed, and says they will know he is among Israel and is the LORD their God.

l: fast and solemn assembly, The Book of Joel, Chapter 2
s: The LORD calls for turning to him with all the heart, with fasting, weeping, and mourning, and says to tear the heart rather than garments. The motive given is that he is gracious, merciful, slow to anger, abundant in loving kindness, and relents from calamity. A fast is sanctified, a solemn assembly is called, and the priests weep between the porch and the altar, asking him to spare his people.

l: outpouring of the Spirit, The Book of Joel, Chapter 2
s: The LORD promises that afterward he will pour out his Spirit on all flesh. Sons and daughters will prophesy, old men will dream dreams, young men will see visions, and the Spirit will also be poured out on servants and handmaids in those days.

l: restoration of harvest and rain, The Book of Joel, Chapter 2
s: The LORD promises grain, new wine, and oil, and tells the land and animals not to fear as pastures spring up and the fig tree and vine yield. He gives the early and latter rain, fills the threshing floors with wheat and the vats with wine and oil, and restores the years eaten by the locust, grasshopper, and caterpillar. The people will eat plenty, be satisfied, and praise the LORD who dealt wondrously with them.

l: The Book of Joel, The Book of Joel, Chapter 3
s: The LORD announces that when he restores the fortunes of Judah and Jerusalem, he will gather all nations into the valley of Jehoshaphat and judge them for scattering Israel, dividing the land, casting lots for his people, and selling them. Tyre, Sidon, and the regions of Philistia are singled out for taking silver, gold, and treasures and for selling Judah's and Jerusalem's children to the Greeks, and the LORD promises to repay them by having Judah's people sell their sons and daughters to Sheba. The nations are summoned to war, to beat plowshares into swords, and to come to the valley of decision, where the LORD will judge them and the harvest and wine press of their wickedness are ripe. The sun, moon, and stars darken as the LORD roars from Zion, yet he is a refuge to his people. The chapter ends with promises that Jerusalem will be holy, the land will flow with wine, milk, and water, Egypt and Edom will become desolate for shedding innocent blood, and Judah will be inhabited forever because the LORD dwells in Zion.

l: LORD, The Book of Joel, Chapter 3
s: The LORD declares he will restore Judah and Jerusalem, gather all nations to the valley of Jehoshaphat, and judge them for what they did to his people. He roars from Zion, shakes heaven and earth, and is a refuge and stronghold to Israel, promising to cleanse their blood and dwell in Zion.

l: Judah, The Book of Joel, Chapter 3
s: Judah's children were sold to the Greeks by Tyre, Sidon, and Philistia, but the LORD will stir them up from where they were sold and have them sell their enemies' sons and daughters to Sheba. Judah will be inhabited forever, its brooks will flow with water, and Egypt and Edom will be desolate for violence done to it.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Joel, Chapter 3
s: Jerusalem's children were sold to the Greeks, but its fortunes will be restored. It will become holy, with no strangers passing through, and will be inhabited from generation to generation.

l: Israel, The Book of Joel, Chapter 3
s: Israel is called the LORD's people and heritage, whom the nations scattered and whose land they divided. The LORD will be a stronghold to the children of Israel.

l: nations, The Book of Joel, Chapter 3
s: The nations are accused of scattering Israel, dividing the land, casting lots for the people, and trading boys and girls for prostitutes and wine. They are summoned to war and to the valley of Jehoshaphat, where the LORD will judge them for their great wickedness.

l: valley of Jehoshaphat, The Book of Joel, Chapter 3
s: The valley of Jehoshaphat is the place where the LORD will bring all nations down and sit to judge them. It is also called the valley of decision, filled with multitudes, where the day of the LORD is near.

l: Zion, The Book of Joel, Chapter 3
s: Zion is the LORD's holy mountain, where he dwells, and from which he will roar. A fountain will flow out from the LORD's house to water the valley of Shittim.

l: day of the LORD, The Book of Joel, Chapter 3
s: The LORD will execute judgment on the nations in the valley of Jehoshaphat, imaged as a sickle put to a ripe harvest and a full wine press. Tyre, Sidon, and Philistia will have their repayment returned on their own heads, and Egypt and Edom will become desolate for shedding innocent blood.

l: restoration of Judah and Jerusalem, The Book of Joel, Chapter 3
s: The restoration is the time the LORD announces when he will restore the fortunes of Judah and Jerusalem, prompting the judgment of the nations. It is described as Jerusalem becoming holy, the land flowing with sweet wine, milk, and waters, and Judah and Jerusalem enduring forever.

l: Jonah, Jonah, The Book of Jonah / Chapter 1
s: The LORD commands Jonah, son of Amittai, to go to Nineveh and preach against its wickedness, but Jonah instead boards a ship at Joppa bound for Tarshish to flee the LORD's presence. The LORD sends a great wind and storm, and the frightened mariners cry to their gods and throw cargo overboard while Jonah sleeps below. When lots identify Jonah as the cause, he tells them he fears the LORD, the God who made the sea and dry land, and asks to be thrown into the sea. After rowing hard in vain, the mariners pray to the LORD and throw Jonah overboard, and the sea stops raging. The mariners fear the LORD, offer a sacrifice and make vows, and the LORD prepares a huge fish that swallows Jonah for three days and three nights.

l: Jonah, Jonah, The Book of Jonah / Chapter 1
s: Jonah, son of Amittai, is told by the LORD to go preach against Nineveh but flees toward Tarshish by ship, sleeping in the ship's innermost parts during the storm. Singled out by lot, he identifies himself as a Hebrew who fears the LORD and tells the mariners to throw him into the sea. He is thrown overboard and swallowed by a huge fish, in whose belly he stays three days and three nights.

l: LORD, Jonah, The Book of Jonah / Chapter 1
s: The LORD commands Jonah to go to Nineveh because its wickedness has come up before him. He sends a great wind and mighty storm after Jonah flees, calms the sea once Jonah is thrown in, and prepares a huge fish to swallow Jonah. The mariners come to fear him exceedingly, sacrifice to him and make vows.

l: Nineveh, Jonah, The Book of Jonah / Chapter 1
s: Nineveh is called a great city whose wickedness has come up before the LORD. The LORD tells Jonah to go there and preach against it, but Jonah does not go in this unit.

l: Tarshish, Jonah, The Book of Jonah / Chapter 1
s: Tarshish is the destination of the ship Jonah boards at Joppa, chosen as the place to flee from the LORD's presence. Jonah never arrives there in this unit.

l: ship (Jonah's ship to Tarshish), Jonah, The Book of Jonah / Chapter 1
s: Jonah pays the fare and boards the ship at Joppa, going down into it to travel to Tarshish. The storm makes it likely to break up, and the crew throw its cargo into the sea to lighten it.

l: mariners (on the ship), Jonah, The Book of Jonah / Chapter 1
s: The mariners are afraid in the storm, each crying to his own god, and they throw the cargo overboard. They cast lots, which fall on Jonah, question him, and row hard to reach land without success. They pray to the LORD not to be guilty of innocent blood, throw Jonah into the sea, and then fear the LORD, offer a sacrifice and make vows. Their ship master wakes Jonah and urges him to call on his God.

l: storm (sent by the LORD), Jonah, The Book of Jonah / Chapter 1
s: The LORD sends a great wind that causes a mighty storm on the sea, threatening to break up the ship. It grows more and more stormy while the men try to row to land, and Jonah says it is on them because of him. It ends when Jonah is thrown into the sea.

l: sea, Jonah, The Book of Jonah / Chapter 1
s: The sea is where the LORD sends the storm, and Jonah describes the LORD as the God who made it and the dry land. It grows more and more stormy until the mariners throw Jonah into it, whereupon it ceases its raging.

l: fish (prepared by the LORD), Jonah, The Book of Jonah / Chapter 1
s: The LORD prepares a huge fish to swallow Jonah. Jonah remains in its belly three days and three nights.

l: Jonah, Jonah, Chapter 2
s: Chapter 2 presents Jonah's prayer to the LORD, his God, from inside the fish's belly. Jonah recounts his affliction, how the LORD threw him into the depths of the seas where waves, weeds, and the deep surrounded him, and how he felt banished yet resolved to look again toward the LORD's holy temple. He says the LORD brought his life up from the pit, and that when his soul fainted he remembered the LORD. He contrasts those who regard vain idols with himself, vowing to sacrifice with thanksgiving and declaring that salvation belongs to the LORD. At the end, the LORD speaks to the fish, and it vomits Jonah onto dry land.

l: Jonah, Jonah, Chapter 2
s: Jonah prays to the LORD, his God, from the fish's belly, describing his affliction, his descent into the depths, and his being brought up from the pit. He remembers the LORD when his soul faints, vows to sacrifice with thanksgiving and pay what he has vowed, and declares that salvation belongs to the LORD. He is then vomited out by the fish onto dry land.

l: LORD, Jonah, Chapter 2
s: The LORD is addressed as Jonah's God, who answered his call and heard his voice from the belly of Sheol. Jonah says the LORD threw him into the depths and brought his life up from the pit, and that salvation belongs to the LORD. The LORD speaks to the fish, which vomits Jonah onto dry land.

l: fish (prepared by the LORD), Jonah, Chapter 2
s: The fish holds Jonah in its belly, where he prays to the LORD. When the LORD speaks to it, it vomits Jonah out onto the dry land.

l: Jonah's prayer, Jonah, Chapter 2
s: Jonah's prayer, spoken from the fish's belly, recounts his cry in affliction, the LORD's answer, his sinking into the deep, and his rescue from the pit. It includes his remembering the LORD when his soul fainted, his claim that his prayer came to the LORD's holy temple, a remark that those who regard vain idols forsake their own mercy, and a vow to sacrifice with thanksgiving, ending with the declaration that salvation belongs to the LORD.

l: Jonah, Jonah, Chapter 3
s: The LORD's word comes to Jonah a second time, commanding him to go to Nineveh and preach the message given to him. Jonah obeys, enters the exceedingly great city, and cries out that Nineveh will be overthrown in forty days. The people of Nineveh believe God and proclaim a fast and put on sackcloth, from greatest to least. The king of Nineveh removes his royal robe, sits in ashes, and decrees that people and animals fast, wear sackcloth, cry to God, and turn from evil and violence, hoping God might relent. God sees their works, relents of the disaster he had threatened, and does not carry it out.

l: Jonah, Jonah, Chapter 3
s: Jonah receives the LORD's word a second time, arises, and goes to Nineveh as commanded. He enters the city a day's journey and cries out that Nineveh will be overthrown in forty days.

l: Nineveh, Jonah, Chapter 3
s: Nineveh is described as an exceedingly great city, three days' journey across. It is warned of overthrow in forty days, repents, and is spared when God relents.

l: LORD, Jonah, Chapter 3
s: The LORD speaks to Jonah a second time, commanding him to go to Nineveh and preach the message he gives. He sees the Ninevites' works in turning from their evil way, relents of the disaster he had said he would do, and does not do it.

l: people of Nineveh (inhabitants), Jonah, Chapter 3
s: The people of Nineveh believe God and proclaim a fast and put on sackcloth, from the greatest to the least. They turn from their evil way, and God sees their works and spares them.

l: king of Nineveh, Jonah, Chapter 3
s: The king of Nineveh hears the news, leaves his throne, takes off his royal robe, covers himself with sackcloth, and sits in ashes. With his nobles he decrees a fast for all people and animals, calls for crying mightily to God and turning from evil and violence, and voices hope that God may relent.

l: message of judgment (Jonah's preaching), Jonah, Chapter 3
s: Jonah's message is a single cry: "In forty days, Nineveh will be overthrown!" It leads the people of Nineveh to believe God and repent.

l: fast and sackcloth repentance, Jonah, Chapter 3
s: The people proclaim a fast and put on sackcloth, and the king extends it by decree to man and animal, herd and flock, who are to taste nothing, drink no water, wear sackcloth, and cry mightily to God. It is joined with turning from evil ways and violence, and God sees these works and relents.

l: disaster (God's threatened judgment), Jonah, Chapter 3
s: The disaster is the overthrow of Nineveh that God said he would do to them. Because the Ninevites turn from their evil way, God relents and does not carry it out.

l: Jonah, Jonah, Chapter 4
s: Jonah is displeased and angry, and prays to the LORD that he fled to Tarshish because he knew God is gracious, merciful, slow to anger, and relents of doing harm; he asks to die. The LORD asks whether it is right for him to be angry. Jonah leaves the city, builds a booth on its east side, and waits to see what will happen to Nineveh. God prepares a vine to shade him, which makes Jonah glad, then prepares a worm that withers it and a sultry east wind, so Jonah grows faint and again asks to die. God asks if he is right to be angry about the vine, and Jonah says he is, even to death. God contrasts Jonah's concern for the vine, which he did not labor for, with His own concern for Nineveh, its more than 120,000 people who cannot discern right from left, and its many animals.

l: Jonah, Jonah, Chapter 4
s: Jonah is displeased and angry, prays that the LORD take his life, and explains that he fled to Tarshish because he knew God is gracious and merciful. He sits in a booth east of the city to watch what becomes of Nineveh, is glad for the vine, then faints in the heat and again asks to die, insisting he is right to be angry even to death.

l: LORD, Jonah, Chapter 4
s: The LORD questions Jonah's anger, then prepares a vine, a worm, and a sultry east wind to teach him. He closes by asking whether He should not be concerned for Nineveh, its many people, and its animals.

l: Nineveh, Jonah, Chapter 4
s: Nineveh is the city Jonah leaves and watches from the east side, waiting to see what will become of it. God calls it that great city, with more than one hundred twenty thousand persons and many animals, and says He should be concerned for it.

l: vine (Jonah's shade), Jonah, Chapter 4
s: God prepares a vine that comes up over Jonah to shade his head and relieve his discomfort, making him exceedingly glad. A worm God prepares at dawn chews it so that it withers; God notes it came up in a night and perished in a night, and Jonah did not labor for it or make it grow.

l: people of Nineveh (inhabitants), Jonah, Chapter 4
s: The inhabitants number more than one hundred twenty thousand persons who cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand. God cites them, along with the animals, as the reason He is concerned for the city.

l: Jonah's anger, Jonah, Chapter 4
s: Jonah's anger arises because the LORD relents of harm, and the LORD asks whether it is right. After the vine withers, Jonah says he is right to be angry even to death, and God contrasts his concern for the vine with His concern for Nineveh.

l: God's mercy and compassion, Jonah, Chapter 4
s: Jonah names God as gracious, merciful, slow to anger, abundant in loving kindness, and one who relents of doing harm. God shows this concern by arguing that He should be concerned for Nineveh's many people and animals, just as Jonah cared about the vine.

l: The Book of Ezra
s: The Book of Ezra, in ten chapters, tells of the return of God's people from Babylonian captivity to Jerusalem, the rebuilding of the temple, and the later restoration of the community under Ezra. It opens in Cyrus's first year, when the LORD stirs Cyrus to proclaim that a house be built in Jerusalem. Heads of households from Judah and Benjamin, priests, and Levites go up, neighbors give gifts, and Cyrus returns the vessels Nebuchadnezzar had taken, counting them to Sheshbazzar, who brings them to Jerusalem. Chapter 2 lists the returnees under leaders including Zerubbabel and Jeshua, totaling 42,360, and notes priestly families disqualified for lack of genealogy. In chapter 3 Jeshua and Zerubbabel build the altar, keep the feast of booths, and lay the temple foundation, amid praise and the mingled weeping and shouting of old men who remembered the first house. Chapters 4 to 6 recount opposition and vindication. Adversaries whose offer of help was refused trouble the builders, and under Artaxerxes a letter from Rehum and Shimshai leads to a royal order stopping the work until Darius's second year. Haggai and Zechariah then prophesy, and building resumes. When Tattenai questions the builders and writes to Darius, a search finds Cyrus's decree at Achmetha. Darius reaffirms it, orders Tattenai to support the Jews, and the house is finished in his sixth year, dedicated with joy, and followed by the Passover. From chapter 7 the focus shifts to Ezra, a priest descended from Aaron and a skilled scribe in the law of Moses. In Artaxerxes' seventh year he travels from Babylon to Jerusalem with the king's letter granting silver, gold, supplies, tribute exemptions for temple personnel, and authority to appoint judges. Chapter 8 lists those who went with him, describes recruiting Levites and temple servants at Casiphia, and a fast at Ahava for a safe way. It then records the weighing of the treasure to twelve priestly chiefs, deliverance from enemies, and safe arrival in Jerusalem, where the treasure was delivered to Meremoth. In chapter 9 the princes report intermarriage with surrounding peoples, including by priests and Levites. Ezra tears his garment, mourns, and prays a confession, calling the LORD righteous. In chapter 10 the weeping assembly, prompted by Shecaniah, covenants to put away foreign wives and their children. A summons gathers the exiles in Jerusalem, and despite some opposition, cases are examined from the tenth month to the first month of the next year, and the book closes by listing those found to have married foreign women.

l: Cyrus, The Book of Ezra
s: Cyrus is a king of Persia, also called king of Babylon, who rules Persia and is said to have been given all the earth's kingdoms by the LORD. In his first year the LORD stirred his spirit, and he issued a written proclamation across his kingdom commissioning him to build a house in Jerusalem. He had the temple vessels counted out to Sheshbazzar, whom he appointed governor, with instructions to place them in the Jerusalem temple. Later, the elders cite his decree, and a scroll found at Achmetha confirms it, ordering expenses paid from the king's house and the vessels restored. His decree is named as an authority behind the completed building.

l: LORD, The Book of Ezra
s: The LORD is the God of heaven and God of Israel, portrayed throughout the Book of Ezra as the deity who dwells in Jerusalem, where he has caused his name to dwell, and who is praised as good, righteous, and enduring in loving kindness toward Israel. In Chapter 1 he fulfills his word spoken through Jeremiah by stirring the spirit of Cyrus and of the heads of households, priests, and Levites to go up and build a house for him. In Chapter 3 he receives burnt and free will offerings and is praised at the foundation laying, as the people follow the law of Moses and David's directions. In Chapter 5 Haggai and Zechariah prophesy in his name, and his eye on the elders keeps officials from stopping the building, though the elders recall that in wrath he gave their fathers into Nebuchadnezzar's hand. In Chapter 6 the decree supplies sacrifices and prayer for the king's life, and Darius invokes him against anyone who alters the decree. In Chapter 7 his good hand is on Ezra and secures the king's favor, while Artaxerxes' letter speaks of wrath against the realm if his commands are neglected. In Chapter 8 he grants the request of those who fasted at Ahava and delivers the company from enemies and bandits; his hand is for good on those who seek him, and his power and wrath are against those who forsake him. In Chapter 9 he is addressed as righteous, having left a remnant and not forsaken Israel in bondage, and as the one who commanded through the prophets against intermarriage, having punished less than iniquities deserved. In Chapter 10 the people, having trespassed against him, seek to turn aside his fierce wrath and make a covenant to do his pleasure.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Ezra
s: Jerusalem, a city in Judah, is the central place in the Book of Ezra's records, containing the house of God and described as the habitation of the God of Israel. It begins as the site where, under Cyrus's proclamation, the LORD's house is to be built; Sheshbazzar brings the vessels there. Exiles return from Babylon, gather in the seventh month, build the altar, and start work on God's house in the second year. In Chapter 4 an accusation letter calls it a rebellious, bad city that would withhold tribute if rebuilt. Artaxerxes' search of the records confirms past insurrections and its former mighty kings, who ruled the whole country beyond the River, and he forbids building until he decrees otherwise. Later, in Artaxerxes' seventh year, Ezra and a company of priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers and temple servants arrive. They rest three days, weigh the offering in God's house, make burnt offerings, and deliver the king's commissions to governors who support the people and the house. The records end with the men of Judah and Benjamin gathering trembling before God's house in heavy rain.

l: Sheshbazzar, The Book of Ezra
s: Sheshbazzar is a prince of Judah entrusted with the LORD's house vessels. Mithredath the treasurer counted them out to him at Cyrus's order, and he brought them up from Babylon to Jerusalem with the captives. Later the elders recall that Cyrus made him governor, told him to place the vessels in the temple, and that he laid the foundations of God's house.

l: Israel, The Book of Ezra
s: Israel is the covenant people, called the children of Israel, whose story here moves from restoration to failure and repentance. They gather as one at Jerusalem in the seventh month, keep the feast of booths, and shout praise when the temple foundation is laid. They later dedicate the house with joy and large offerings, and keep the Passover with others who separated from the nations' filthiness. Some, including priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers and temple servants, go up with Ezra under Artaxerxes' decree. Ezra then learns that the people, priests and Levites have not separated from the peoples of the lands and have taken their daughters as wives. His prayer calls them a guilty remnant, once delivered to kings, sword, captivity and plunder, yet revived and allowed to rebuild. Their guilt is increased by foreign marriages. All Israel swears to follow Ezra's plan, a great assembly weeps bitterly, and many families are listed as having taken foreign wives.

l: house of God at Jerusalem, The Book of Ezra
s: The house of God at Jerusalem is the temple of the LORD, first built long ago by a great king of Israel and later destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar after the fathers provoked God to wrath. The records follow its rebuilding. Cyrus declared that the LORD commanded him to build it and invited God's people to go up; heads of households, priests, and Levites responded, supported by silver, gold, goods, animals, and freewill offerings. Offerings began in the seventh month before the foundation was laid. Materials such as cedar from Lebanon were arranged, and work began in the second month of the second year, after which the foundation was laid with praise; Sheshbazzar is also named as having laid its foundations. Adversaries who offered help were refused and then opposed it, and after Artaxerxes' order construction stopped until the second year of Darius. Zerubbabel and Jeshua resumed building with great stones and timber in the walls, though it was not yet complete. Under the decrees of Cyrus and Darius, with royal funding and the return of its vessels, the elders finished it on the third day of Adar in Darius's sixth year. It was dedicated with joy and sacrifices, and priests and Levites were set in divisions. Later, Ezra was to carry gifts for it, offerings were to be bought for its altar, its personnel were exempt from tribute, and the king's heart was praised for beautifying it.

l: heads of fathers' households (of Judah and Benjamin), The Book of Ezra
s: has_spirit_stirred_by God [to go up and build the LORD's house] The heads of fathers' households of Judah and Benjamin, together with the priests and Levites, rose up to go to Jerusalem and build the LORD's house, because God had stirred their spirits. Those around them strengthened their hands with vessels of silver, gold, goods, animals, and precious things.

l: priests, The Book of Ezra
s: Twelve of the chiefs of the priests, including Sherebiah and Hashabiah, were set apart to receive the silver, gold, and vessels, and were told they and the vessels were holy to the LORD. In Jerusalem the treasure was weighed into the hand of Meremoth the son of Uriah the priest, with Eleazar son of Phinehas.

l: Levites, The Book of Ezra
s: Levites, a group of 74 descendants of Jeshua, Kadmiel and Hodaviah, were initially absent at Ahava; Iddo at Casiphia sent Sherebiah, Hashabiah, kin and 220 temple servants. In Jerusalem Levites witnessed the treasure weighing and were purified with the priests.

l: captives (brought up from Babylon), The Book of Ezra
s: brought_up_from Babylon [to Jerusalem] The captives were brought up from Babylon to Jerusalem. Sheshbazzar brought the vessels of the LORD's house up at that time.

l: gold and silver vessels of God's house, The Book of Ezra
s: A collection of five thousand four hundred gold and silver vessels from God's house. Nebuchadnezzar took them from the Jerusalem temple to Babylon and placed them in the house of his gods. Cyrus later brought them out and had them counted to Sheshbazzar, who brought them up to Jerusalem.

l: Cyrus's proclamation, The Book of Ezra
s: invites people of God [to go up to Jerusalem and build the house of the LORD] The proclamation was made throughout Cyrus's kingdom and put in writing. It stated that the LORD had given Cyrus all the kingdoms and commanded him to build a house in Jerusalem, invited any of God's people to go up and build, and directed that those remaining in any place help the travelers with silver, gold, goods, and animals, in addition to the freewill offering for God's house.

l: Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, The Book of Ezra
s: Zerubbabel, son of Shealtiel, is a leader of the people returning from captivity. Named first among the returnees alongside Jeshua, he builds the altar of the God of Israel with his relatives and Jeshua, offers burnt offerings, and begins work on the LORD's house under Cyrus's command. Finally, with Jeshua and the household heads, he refuses the adversaries' offer of help, insisting they alone will build.

l: Jeshua the son of Jozadak, The Book of Ezra
s: Jeshua, son of Jozadak, is a priest who stood with Zerubbabel and his fellow priests to build the altar of the God of Israel and offer burnt offerings per the law of Moses. In the second year he helped oversee the house's work. His priestly sons had married foreign women.

l: Rehum, The Book of Ezra
s: Rehum, chancellor living in Samaria, writes with Shimshai the scribe to Artaxerxes against Jerusalem, receives the king's order to stop the building, then hurries there to forcibly halt the Jews.

l: returning exiles (children of the province), The Book of Ezra
s: The returning exiles, children of the province, were people carried to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar who came back under Zerubbabel's leadership. They returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to his own city, totaling 42,360 plus 7,337 servants and 200 singers, with 736 horses, 245 mules, 435 camels, and 6,720 donkeys. Priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, temple servants and all Israel settled in their cities.

l: priests (Jeshua's brothers), The Book of Ezra
s: The priests, Jeshua's brothers, are registered by family: Jedaiah (973), Immer (1,052), Pashhur (1,247), and Harim (1,017). Families of Habaiah, Hakkoz, and Barzillai could not prove their genealogy and were disqualified from the priesthood, barred from the most holy things until a priest with Urim and Thummim arose. The priests gave 100 garments to the treasury, then stood with Jeshua to build the altar and, at the foundation, praised the LORD with trumpets, many weeping.

l: freewill offering for the temple, The Book of Ezra
s: Some heads of fathers' households willingly gave, according to their ability, to the treasury for setting up God's house: 61,000 darics of gold, 5,000 minas of silver, and 100 priests' garments.

l: return from Babylonian captivity, The Book of Ezra
s: Those whom Nebuchadnezzar had carried away to Babylon went up out of captivity and returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to his own city, with Zerubbabel and other leaders. Some who came from Tel Melah, Tel Harsha, Cherub, Addan, and Immer could not show their fathers' houses or prove they were of Israel. The return ends with the people settled in their cities.

l: census of returnees, The Book of Ezra
s: A census of returnees totals the whole assembly at 42,360, with 7,337 servants and 200 singers counted separately. Chapter 2 lists men of Israel by family and town, then priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, temple servants, ending with livestock totals.

l: Levites, The Book of Ezra
s: oversee temple of the LORD (foundation) [from twenty years old and upward] Levites from twenty years old and upward were appointed to oversee the work of the LORD's house, and Kadmiel, the sons of Judah, and the sons of Henadad with their sons and brothers oversaw the workmen. The Levites, the sons of Asaph, played cymbals to praise the LORD at the foundation laying.

l: altar of the God of Israel, The Book of Ezra
s: An altar of the God of Israel, built by Jeshua, Zerubbabel and companions per the law of Moses, set on its base despite fear of surrounding peoples, then used for morning and evening burnt offerings.

l: burnt offerings, The Book of Ezra
s: are_offered_to LORD [morning and evening] Burnt offerings were offered on the altar morning and evening, starting from the first day of the seventh month, along with the daily offerings by number, the continual offering, the new moon offerings, the set feasts, and free will offerings. They began before the temple foundation was laid.

l: law of Moses, The Book of Ezra
s: given_by LORD (God of Israel) The law of Moses is described as given by the LORD, the God of Israel, and Ezra is a skilled scribe in it. The letter refers to it as the law of Ezra's God, which is in his hand, and Ezra is to use it to inquire about Judah and Jerusalem and to appoint judges who know it. Ezra is also to teach those who do not know it, and those who will not do it face judgment.

l: Jews, The Book of Ezra
s: The Jews are the returned captives in Judah and Jerusalem who worship the God of Israel. They build a temple, reject outside help, and are weakened by the people of the land until forced to stop. Prophets Haggai and Zechariah encourage them, and the work continues while Tattenai's inquiry goes to Darius. Later they are charged with trespass by marrying foreign women, are summoned to Jerusalem, and examine each case while Ezra mourns.

l: old men who had seen the first house, The Book of Ezra
s: has_attribute saw the first house [included priests, Levites, heads of fathers’ households] Many of the priests, Levites, and heads of fathers' households who were old men and had seen the first house wept with a loud voice when they saw the new foundation laid. Their weeping mingled with the joyful shouting of others.

l: foundation laying celebration, The Book of Ezra
s: A celebration at the laying of the foundation: priests with trumpets and Levites with cymbals praise the LORD, people sing antiphonally of his goodness and enduring kindness, and joyful shouting mingles indistinguishably with weeping, heard far away.

l: adversaries of Judah and Benjamin, The Book of Ezra
s: The adversaries of Judah and Benjamin, called the people of the land, ask to join temple building, claiming they seek Israel's God and have sacrificed since Esar Haddon's days. Zerubbabel rejects them, after which they weaken Judah's hands, trouble the builders, and hire counselors to frustrate the work.

l: Darius the king, The Book of Ezra
s: Darius, king of Persia, has the archives searched, finds Cyrus's decree scroll, and issues his own confirming it, ordering governors beyond the River to fund the work and threatening alterers; the house is finished in his sixth year.

l: Artaxerxes, The Book of Ezra
s: Artaxerxes is a Persian king who styles himself king of kings and is advised by seven counselors. In Chapter 4, after receiving Rehum and Shimshai's letter, he searches the records, finds Jerusalem's rebellious past, and orders construction halted until he decrees otherwise. In Chapter 7, in his seventh year, he reverses course for Ezra: permitting Israelites to go, funding them from the treasury, exempting temple personnel from tribute, and enforcing God's law and his own.

l: Shimshai, The Book of Ezra
s: has_title scribe Shimshai the scribe joins Rehum in writing the letter against Jerusalem to Artaxerxes. He is addressed in the king's reply and helps enforce the stop order at Jerusalem.

l: companions of Rehum and Shimshai, The Book of Ezra
s: lives_in Samaria Named as the Dinaites, Apharsathchites, Tarpelites, Apharsites, Archevites, Babylonians, Shushanchites, Dehaites, Elamites, and the rest of the nations Osnappar settled in Samaria and beyond the River, they join in writing the letter. They go in haste to Jerusalem after the king's reply and stop the Jews by force of arms.

l: letter of accusation to Artaxerxes, The Book of Ezra
s: A Syrian-language letter by Rehum, Shimshai, and companions accusing the Jews of rebuilding walls and foundations, warning the king of losing his land beyond the River, urging a records search; it prompts Artaxerxes to order building halted.

l: stopping of the temple work, The Book of Ezra
s: Work on God's house in Jerusalem halts after Artaxerxes' letter is read to Rehum, Shimshai and companions, who go and stop the Jews by force of arms; it stays stopped until Darius's second year.

l: Tattenai, The Book of Ezra
s: Tattenai is a governor beyond the River who, with Shetharbozenai and their companions, questions the Jews about who authorized their building and the builders' names, then writes to Darius asking for a search for Cyrus's decree. Darius's decree orders him to stay away and fund the elders, and he complies diligently.

l: elders of the Jews, The Book of Ezra
s: The elders of the Jews are builders of God's house at Jerusalem. Watched over by God, they are not stopped; they answer Tattenai, citing Cyrus's decree. Authorized and funded from the king's goods, they prosper through Haggai's and Zechariah's prophesying and finish the temple.

l: Darius, The Book of Ezra
s: is_a king Darius is the king to whom Tattenai and his companions send their letter. He is asked to search the king's treasure house at Babylon for Cyrus's decree and to send his pleasure concerning the matter.

l: letter to Darius, The Book of Ezra
s: A letter from Tattenai, Shetharbozenai and the Apharsachites to Darius, greeting him, reporting diligent house-building, relaying the elders' claim of Cyrus's decree, and requesting a search of Babylon's treasure house.

l: decree to build the house, The Book of Ezra
s: A decree issued in Cyrus's first year orders the house of God built at Jerusalem, sixty cubits high and wide, with its expenses paid from the king's house and the gold and silver vessels of God's house restored. In Chapter 5 the Jewish elders cite it, and Tattenai's letter asks that Babylon's treasure house be searched. In Chapter 6 the decree is found in a scroll at Achmetha in Media, Darius confirms it, and the building is completed according to it.

l: dedication of the temple, The Book of Ezra
s: The temple's dedication is a joyful ceremony by the children of Israel, priests, Levites and the rest of the captivity. They offer 100 bulls, 200 rams, 400 lambs and 12 male goats for the tribes, then set priests and Levites in their divisions per Moses' book.

l: Passover, The Book of Ezra
s: observed_on fourteenth day of the first month [by children of the captivity] The children of the captivity keep the Passover on the fourteenth day of the first month. The priests and Levites had purified themselves and killed the Passover for all the returned exiles, their brothers the priests, and themselves. It is followed by seven days of the feast of unleavened bread with joy.

l: Ezra, The Book of Ezra
s: Ezra is a priest and scribe skilled in the law of Moses, son of Seraiah and a descendant of Aaron through Phinehas and Eleazar. He set his heart to seek and do the LORD's law and to teach it in Israel, and the LORD's hand was upon him. The records follow his course from commission to reform. In the reign of Artaxerxes he goes up from Babylon to Jerusalem, authorized by the king to appoint magistrates and judges for the people beyond the River and to carry offerings. He gathers households at the river Ahava, finds no Levites, sends to Iddo for ministers, proclaims a fast to seek a straight way from God, entrusts the offering to twelve priestly chiefs, and leads the group to Jerusalem, where he delivers the king's commissions. Later, hearing the princes' report of the people's trespass, he tears his garment and robe, pulls out hair, and sits confounded until the evening offering. He then prays and confesses the people's guilt, weeps before God's house, has leaders swear to carry out Shecaniah's proposal, and calls the people to confess and separate from the foreign women.

l: silver, gold, and vessels offering, The Book of Ezra
s: A holy free will offering to God for the house of God, given by the king, his counselors, his princes, and all Israel present. It consisted of 650 talents of silver, 100 talents of silver vessels, 100 talents of gold, twenty gold bowls weighing 1,000 darics, and two vessels of fine bright bronze. In Chapter 7 the king and counselors freely give silver and gold, which Ezra is to carry, along with other offerings, to buy altar offerings; treasurers beyond the River may supply more. In Chapter 8 the gifts are weighed at Ahava, guarded by priests and Levites, then weighed again in Jerusalem into Meremoth's hand, counted and recorded.

l: Ezra's journey to Jerusalem, The Book of Ezra
s: Ezra's journey from Babylon to Jerusalem, a four-month trip in the seventh year of Artaxerxes, credited to God's good hand upon him. He set out on the first day of the first month with Israelites, priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, temple servants, and gathered chief men, arriving the first day of the fifth month.

l: Artaxerxes' letter, The Book of Ezra
s: A royal decree authored by Artaxerxes and addressed to Ezra the priest and scribe. It permits willing Israelites, priests, and Levites to accompany him, sends him to inquire about Judah and Jerusalem, orders supplies from treasurers, exempts temple workers from taxes, appoints magistrates and judges, and prescribes penalties for disobedience.

l: Shecaniah the son of Jehiel, The Book of Ezra
s: Shecaniah, son of Jehiel and one of the sons of Elam, confesses to Ezra that the people trespassed by marrying foreign women, yet sees hope; he proposes a covenant to put away wives and children and urges Ezra to act.

l: Ahava river, The Book of Ezra
s: is_a river [runs to Ahava] The river that runs to Ahava is where the narrator gathered the returning company and they encamped three days. There he found no Levites, proclaimed the fast, and weighed out the offering, and the company departed from it on the twelfth day of the first month.

l: Sherebiah, The Book of Ezra
s: Sherebiah, a discreet Levite of the sons of Mahli, was brought from Casiphia with his sons and brothers, eighteen in all, then set apart as one of twelve priestly chiefs to receive the weighed silver, gold, and vessels.

l: Hashabiah, The Book of Ezra
s: Hashabiah is a man who came with Jeshaiah of the sons of Merari, plus brothers and sons, twenty in all, and was set apart with Sherebiah and ten brothers as one of twelve chiefs entrusted with the offering.

l: fast at Ahava, The Book of Ezra
s: A fast proclaimed by the narrator at the river Ahava, where the people humbled themselves to seek a straight way for themselves, children, and possessions, after his shame at asking the king for soldiers; God granted their plea.

l: returning exiles, The Book of Ezra
s: The children of the captivity are exiles who came out of Babylon during Artaxerxes' reign. Heads of households and their males are listed, with counts from fifty to 218. They then offer twelve bulls, ninety-six rams, seventy-seven lambs, and twelve sin-offering goats for all Israel.

l: journey from Ahava to Jerusalem, The Book of Ezra
s: A journey from the river Ahava to Jerusalem, beginning on the twelfth day of the first month. God's hand delivered the company from enemy and bandits en route; they reached Jerusalem and stayed three days before weighing the treasure.

l: princes and rulers, The Book of Ezra
s: has_role_in intermarriage [chief in the trespass] The princes bring the report of the intermarriage to Ezra. They also admit that the hand of the princes and rulers has been chief in this trespass.

l: peoples of the lands, The Book of Ezra
s: has_attribute abominations [filled the land with filthiness] The peoples of the lands are listed as Canaanites, Hittites, Perizzites, Jebusites, Ammonites, Moabites, Egyptians, and Amorites, and are described as following abominations. The prophetic command describes their land as unclean and filled with their filthiness, and forbids seeking their peace or prosperity.

l: intermarriage, The Book of Ezra
s: is_a trespass [taking daughters of the peoples of the lands for themselves and their sons] Israelites, including priests, Levites, princes, and rulers, have taken daughters of the peoples of the lands for themselves and their sons, so that the holy offspring have mixed with those peoples. Ezra and his prayer treat this as a trespass against the prophets' commandment and warn that repeating it would provoke the LORD's anger to the point of consuming the remnant.

l: foreign women, The Book of Ezra
s: is_from peoples of the land The foreign women, taken as wives by many men of Israel, are the cause of the trespass and guilt confessed in the chapter. The covenant calls for them to be put away along with their children, and the text notes that some of the men had children by them.

l: covenant to put away foreign wives, The Book of Ezra
s: A covenant made with God, proposed by Shecaniah, to put away foreign wives and their children according to the law. Ezra has priests, Levites, and all Israel swear to it, and the guilty priests pledge and offer a ram for guilt.

l: assembly at Jerusalem, The Book of Ezra
s: An assembly of Judah and Benjamin men at Jerusalem, in the wide place before God's house, on the twentieth day of the ninth month. Trembling in heavy rain, they hear Ezra's exhortation, answer loudly that they will comply, then request appointed times and leaders to handle the matter; four named men oppose or assist opposition.

l: examination of mixed marriages, The Book of Ezra
s: An examination of men who married foreign women, led by Ezra and heads of fathers' households. It began on the first day of the tenth month and finished by the first day of the first month, naming offenders among priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, and Israelite families, some with children.

l: The Book of Nehemiah
s: The Book of Nehemiah is a first-person and third-person account of Nehemiah, cupbearer to King Artaxerxes, who leads the rebuilding of Jerusalem's wall and the renewal of its community. In chapter 1, in Susa, he hears from his brother Hanani that Jerusalem's wall is broken and its gates burned, and he weeps, fasts, and prays, confessing Israel's sins. In chapter 2 the king, seeing his sadness, grants his request to go to Judah, with letters for safe passage and timber. Nehemiah inspects the walls at night and rallies the Jews, while Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem mock and accuse them. Chapter 3 lists the priests, families, and guilds who repaired each section and gate, noting that the Tekoite nobles would not join the work. Chapter 4 shows opposition growing into a plot to attack; Nehemiah answers with prayer, guards, and armed builders, with a trumpeter to rally the people. Chapter 5 turns to an internal crisis: the poor cry out against nobles who exact usury and take their fields and children. Nehemiah confronts them, secures an oath to restore what was taken, and recalls that in twelve years as governor he took no food allowance. In chapter 6 the enemies try four times to lure him to Ono, send a letter accusing him of rebellion, and hire Shemaiah to frighten him into the temple; he refuses all of it. The wall is finished in fifty-two days, and the nations perceive God's hand, though Tobiah still corresponds with nobles of Judah. Chapter 7 sets Hanani and Hananiah over the city, which is large but sparsely settled, and reproduces the genealogy of the first returnees, totaling 42,360, with gifts given to the work. Chapter 8 centers on Ezra reading the law at the water gate; the people weep, are told that the joy of the LORD is their strength, and celebrate the feast of booths. Chapter 9 is a day of fasting, confession, and a long Levite prayer recounting God's mercy and Israel's rebellion, ending in a written covenant. Chapter 10 lists those who sealed it and their pledges: no intermarriage, Sabbath observance, debt and seventh-year release, and support for the temple. Chapter 11 describes resettling Jerusalem by lot, one in ten, and lists settlements. Chapter 12 lists priests and Levites and describes the wall's dedication, with two thanksgiving processions meeting at God's house. Chapter 13 shows Nehemiah, back from the king, reversing lapses: he removes Tobiah from a temple room, restores the Levites' portions, stops Sabbath trading, and confronts foreign marriages, repeatedly asking God to remember him.

l: Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah
s: Nehemiah, son of Hacaliah and brother of Hanani, is a Jewish cupbearer to King Artaxerxes in Susa who becomes governor of Judah. The records open with him hearing of Jerusalem's affliction and its broken wall; he weeps, fasts, prays, and confesses Israel's sin. Having obtained the king's permission, letters and timber, he travels to Judah, inspects the walls secretly by night, and rallies the people to rebuild, answering mockers by trusting the God of heaven. He faces opposition from Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite, who were grieved that someone sought Israel's welfare. He sets watches, arms the builders by family groups, keeps a trumpeter beside him, and with his brothers, servants and guards does not undress. He confronts the nobles and rulers over usury and has them swear to restore what was taken. Throughout his twelve years as governor, from the twentieth to the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes, he refuses the governor's bread out of fear of God, lends to the people, buys no land, and hosts 150 men at his table. He refuses four invitations to meet at Ono, denies Sanballat's accusation, rejects Shemaiah's advice to hide in the temple, and the wall is finished in fifty-two days. He then appoints Hanani and Hananiah over Jerusalem, sets rules for the gates, and finds the genealogy of the first returnees. Later he is named governor alongside Ezra and the Levites in comforting the people, is first among those sealing the covenant, and leads the thanksgiving companies on the wall. After returning from leave from the king, he finds Tobiah housed in the temple courts and throws out his belongings, has the rooms cleansed, restores the Levites' portions, appoints treasurers, shuts the gates against Sabbath trade, and confronts, curses and strikes men who married foreign women. He repeatedly asks God to remember him for good, a note running from the prayerful opening to the close.

l: Hanani, The Book of Nehemiah
s: Hanani is Nehemiah's faithful, God-fearing brother from Judah. He first arrives with men from Judah, reporting Jerusalem's ruined wall and gates and the remnant's affliction. Later, he is placed in charge of Jerusalem with Hananiah, overseeing the gates and the watches.

l: Judah, The Book of Nehemiah
s: Judah is a people group whose members settled in Jerusalem and in towns from Kiriath Arba and Beersheba to Azekah, encamping toward the valley of Hinnom. Later, all Judah brought tithes once Nehemiah restored order, though some violated the Sabbath and Nehemiah rebuked the nobles of Judah for profaning it.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Nehemiah
s: Jerusalem is a holy city whose fortunes are traced through the Book of Nehemiah, from ruin to restoration. It begins in waste: its wall broken down and its gates burned with fire, a report that moves Nehemiah to weeping, mourning, fasting, and prayer. It is also the place of the narrator's fathers' tombs. He arrives, inspects the broken walls by night, and calls the people to rebuild. The wall and gates (valley, dung, spring) are repaired in divided districts, with rulers Rephaiah son of Hur and Shallum son of Hallohesh each governing half a district; Shallum repaired with his daughters. Enemies conspire against the work, so residents lodge in the city to guard by night and labor by day. With the wall fortified and doors set up, gatekeepers, singers, and Levites are appointed. The city is wide and large but sparsely populated, with houses not yet built, so people chosen by lot, one in ten, settle there. At the dedication, the Levites gather and the joy of the great sacrifices is heard far away. Finally, Nehemiah returns to find Sabbath trade and a misused temple room, and shuts the gates at dusk before the Sabbath.

l: wall of Jerusalem, The Book of Nehemiah
s: The wall of Jerusalem is a structure whose condition changes across the Book of Nehemiah. It first appears broken down, its gates burned with fire, which moves Nehemiah to grief and prayer. He inspects it by night, finding a place where his animal could not pass, and urges the people to rebuild so they will not be disgraced. Despite mockery, the wall is joined together to half its height, and the filled breaches provoke enemy plotting. It is then completed with no breach left on the twenty-fifth of Elul, in fifty-two days, though the gate doors are not yet set up. Its completion frightens surrounding nations, who perceive God as the doer. Finally, priests and Levites purify it, and the princes of Judah and two thanksgiving companies go up on it for the dedication, passing its many gates and towers.

l: sheep gate, The Book of Nehemiah
s: The sheep gate is a gate of Jerusalem, built by Eliashib the high priest and his fellow priests, who sanctified it as far as the towers of Hammeah and Hananel and set up its doors. It marks where the repair account closes, with goldsmiths and merchants working nearby. Later, Nehemiah ordered gates shut over the Sabbath, and Levites were set to guard them.

l: Jews, The Book of Nehemiah
s: The Jews are the remnant living in the province of Judah. They are first reported to Nehemiah as in great affliction and reproach. Later they are mocked as feeble yet keep building because they are willing to work, then, warned of attacks from every direction, they labor armed, half guarding while half build.

l: God, The Book of Nehemiah
s: God, called the LORD and the God of heaven and of Israel, is the central divine figure of these records from the Book of Nehemiah. He is described as great and awesome, keeping covenant and loving kindness with those who love him and keep his commandments, and as gracious, merciful, slow to anger and ready to pardon. He is the sole creator and preserver of heaven, earth, seas and all in them, and he is declared just in all that has come on Israel. The account begins with Nehemiah's address to him, recalling his word to Moses to scatter transgressors and gather the returning, and his redemption of his people by a strong hand. Through the building narrative he is the one prayed to before the king, credited with the good hand that granted Nehemiah's requests, the one who brings enemy counsel to nothing, who is promised to fight for the people, and whose work the nations perceive in the finished wall. He is invoked in oaths, including Nehemiah's shaking out of the lap, and in the fear of God that restrains oppression. Nehemiah repeatedly asks him to remember his good deeds and to remember his opponents for their works. In the reading of the law, he is blessed as the great God, and his joy is the people's strength. The Levites' recital traces his history: choosing Abram, delivering the people from Egypt, giving the law at Sinai through Moses, sustaining them in the wilderness, and giving them the land of Canaan, while repeatedly pardoning a rebellious people, though also giving them into adversaries' hands. The people then vow by oath to keep his commandments and not forsake his house. The close recalls that he turned Balaam's curse into blessing, brought evil for Sabbath violations, loved Solomon, and is appealed to for loving kindness.

l: children of Israel, The Book of Nehemiah
