s: The children of Israel are God's servants, redeemed by his great power and strong hand, yet they have sinned, dealing very corruptly and not keeping the commandments given to Moses. Nehemiah prays and confesses for them. The people gather as one, hear the law read, weep, worship, answer "Amen," celebrate, and dwell in temporary shelters, as had not been done since Joshua's days. They then assemble with fasting, sackcloth, and dirt, separate from foreigners, and confess their own and their fathers' sins. They acknowledge servitude in their own land under kings who rule their bodies and livestock because of sin, and conclude by making a sure written covenant, sealed by princes, Levites, and priests.

l: Nehemiah's prayer, The Book of Nehemiah
s: Nehemiah's prayer to God, day and night, on behalf of the children of Israel. After fasting, he appeals for a hearing, confesses Israel's and his father's house's sins, recalls the word to Moses, and asks for prosperity and mercy before this man.

l: commandments, statutes and ordinances, The Book of Nehemiah
s: The LORD's commandments, statutes and ordinances, given through his servant Moses at Sinai along with the holy Sabbath, give life to those who do them; ancestors refused obedience and discarded the law, and it is then read aloud to the assembly.

l: Artaxerxes, The Book of Nehemiah
s: Artaxerxes is a king with a queen who, in his twentieth year, notices the narrator's sadness, grants his request to go to Judah, and supplies letters to governors, Asaph for timber, and army escorts.

l: Sanballat the Horonite, The Book of Nehemiah
s: Sanballat the Horonite is an adversary of Nehemiah and of the rebuilding of Jerusalem's wall. He is grieved when someone arrives to seek Israel's welfare, then ridicules the builders with Tobiah and Geshem, and is told he has no portion, right or memorial in Jerusalem. Growing angry, he mocks the Jews before the army of Samaria and joins Tobiah, Arabians, Ammonites and Ashdodites in conspiring to attack Jerusalem. He finally tries to lure Nehemiah to Ono four times, sends an open letter alleging rebellion, and hires Shemaiah to frighten him.

l: Tobiah the Ammonite, The Book of Nehemiah
s: Tobiah the Ammonite, called a servant, is a persistent enemy of Nehemiah who opposes the rebuilding of Jerusalem's wall. He begins by being grieved at Israel's welfare, then ridicules the builders alongside Sanballat and Geshem, scoffing that a fox could break the wall, and joins the conspiracy against Jerusalem. After the wall is finished, he hires Shemaiah to frighten Nehemiah and sends intimidating letters. Through marriage ties to Shecaniah and his son Jehohanan's marriage, many in Judah are sworn to him, and nobles correspond with him. Eliashib the priest gives him a temple room, but Nehemiah returns and throws out his belongings.

l: Geshem the Arabian, The Book of Nehemiah
s: is_enemy_of Nehemiah [intended to harm him] Geshem the Arabian is named among the enemies who hear that the wall is built. He joins Sanballat in sending to Nehemiah to propose a meeting in the plain of Ono, though they intended to harm him.

l: God's house, The Book of Nehemiah
s: The house of God was neglected because the Levites' portions were not given and the workers fled to their fields, and its courts held a room for Tobiah. Nehemiah cleansed the rooms, restored the offerings and vessels, and had the people bring tithes to the treasuries again.

l: rebuilding of Jerusalem's wall, The Book of Nehemiah
s: The rebuilding of Jerusalem's wall is a communal project proposed by the narrator after secretly inspecting the wall. The people resolve to rise up and build, backed by the king's letters and timber and by God of heaven, though Sanballat, Tobiah and Geshem mock it. Work is divided into sections among priests, rulers, Levites, craftsmen and townspeople, including the Fish Gate, circling from the Sheep Gate back to it.

l: Eliashib the high priest, The Book of Nehemiah
s: Eliashib is the high priest who first appears leading his fellow priests in building and sanctifying the sheep gate, with his house serving as a landmark for wall repairs by Baruch and Meremoth. Later, as the priest over the rooms of God's house and an ally of Tobiah, he prepares a great temple room, once used for offerings and vessels, for Tobiah. Nehemiah condemns this as evil.

l: priests, The Book of Nehemiah
s: repairs horse gate [above the gate, each across from his own house] The priests, led by Eliashib, built and sanctified the sheep gate and the wall to the towers of Hammeah and Hananel. Later, the priests from the surrounding area made repairs, and the priests repaired above the horse gate, each across from his own house.

l: Tekoites, The Book of Nehemiah
s: The Tekoites are a group who helped rebuild Jerusalem's wall, repairing one section, then a second portion opposite the great tower to the wall of Ophel, though their nobles refused to put their necks to the work.

l: goldsmiths and merchants, The Book of Nehemiah
s: Tyrian men living in Jerusalem and other merchants brought fish and wares to sell on the Sabbath. After the gates were shut they camped outside the wall once or twice, until Nehemiah threatened to lay hands on them and they stopped coming on the Sabbath.

l: adversaries, The Book of Nehemiah
s: intend_to kill the Jews and stop the work Sanballat, Tobiah, the Arabians, the Ammonites, and the Ashdodites mock the builders and then grow very angry as the breaches are filled. They say the Jews will not see them coming until they are among them to kill them and stop the work, but they learn that their plan is known and that God has frustrated it.

l: builders and burden bearers, The Book of Nehemiah
s: carries weapons [work with one hand, hold weapon in the other] The builders and burden bearers work with one hand and hold a weapon with the other, and each builder wears his sword at his side. Half the people hold spears from morning until the stars appear, and they are told to rally to the sound of the trumpet because they are spread far apart on the wall.

l: conspiracy to attack Jerusalem, The Book of Nehemiah
s: targets Jerusalem [to fight and cause confusion] Sanballat, Tobiah, the Arabians, the Ammonites, and the Ashdodites conspire together to come and fight against Jerusalem and cause confusion. They plan to come among the Jews unseen and kill them to stop the work, but the plot is met with prayer, a watch, armed guards, and is brought to nothing when the enemies learn their plan is known.

l: the Jews (Nehemiah's brothers), The Book of Nehemiah
s: Nehemiah's poor Jewish brothers suffer famine and crushing debt bondage, mortgaging fields and houses and surrendering children to servitude; Nehemiah, who had redeemed Jews sold to the nations, argues that selling them again would be wrong.

l: nobles and rulers, The Book of Nehemiah
s: Nobles and rulers who charged usury to their brothers and held the people's mortgaged fields, vineyards and houses. Confronted by Nehemiah in a great assembly, they had no answer, then swore before priests to restore property and charges and demand nothing more.

l: the people, The Book of Nehemiah
s: The people are a community afflicted by famine and the king's tribute, forced to mortgage fields, vineyards and houses and to put their sons and daughters into debt bondage. They cry out over their hardship. Former governors had burdened them with bread, wine and silver, though Nehemiah did not demand the governor's pay. After the nobles' promise, the assembly says Amen, praises the LORD, and keeps the promise.

l: usury, The Book of Nehemiah
s: is_a practice reproached as not good [brings reproach from the nations] Usury was being exacted by the nobles and rulers from their own brothers, and Nehemiah condemned it as not good. He asked that it stop and that the hundredth part of money, grain, new wine, and oil being charged be restored, and the nobles agreed.

l: debt bondage, The Book of Nehemiah
s: affects daughters and sons of the people [servants] Debt bondage is shown in the people's complaint that they were bringing their sons and daughters into servitude, and some daughters were already in bondage, because others held their fields and vineyards. Nehemiah contrasts this with having redeemed Jews sold to the nations, and he says the bondage was heavy on the people.

l: mortgaged property (fields, vineyards, houses), The Book of Nehemiah
s: includes olive groves [to be restored] Fields, vineyards, and houses were mortgaged to get grain during the famine and to pay the king's tribute, and other men came to hold them. Nehemiah demanded that the fields, vineyards, olive groves, and houses be restored that very day, and the nobles and rulers promised to do so.

l: enemies (Nehemiah's enemies), The Book of Nehemiah
s: Nehemiah's enemies try to lure him to Ono, accuse him of rebellion, and hire a prophet to frighten him, all to weaken the work. When the wall is finished, the surrounding nations are afraid and lose their confidence, perceiving the work was done by God.

l: Sanballat's open letter, The Book of Nehemiah
s: An open letter sent by Sanballat through his servant, the fifth delivery, accusing Nehemiah and the Jews of plotting rebellion and kingship, citing rumors, prophets and a threat to inform the king, and demanding a meeting. Nehemiah denies it, calling it Sanballat's invention.

l: Shemaiah, The Book of Nehemiah
s: Shemaiah, son of Delaiah, appears shut in at home and urges Nehemiah to hide in the temple from night assassins. Nehemiah refuses, discerning God did not send him and Tobiah and Sanballat hired him.

l: plot to intimidate Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah
s: aims_to make Nehemiah afraid and sin [to give material for an evil report] The plot includes repeated invitations to Ono, an open letter alleging rebellion, and Shemaiah's hired prophecy urging Nehemiah into the temple so that he would sin and give enemies material for an evil report. Nehemiah rejects each element. Tobiah's letters to put him in fear continue even after the wall is finished.

l: Hananiah, The Book of Nehemiah
s: Hananiah, faithful governor of the fortress who feared God above many, is placed in charge of Jerusalem alongside Hanani in Chapter 7.

l: singers, The Book of Nehemiah
s: The singers are a group responsible for service in God's house. They built villages around Jerusalem, gathered from surrounding areas for the dedication, sang loudly under overseer Jezrahiah, and received daily portions by royal commandment, given by all Israel in Zerubbabel's and Nehemiah's days.

l: priests, The Book of Nehemiah
s: The priests are a group of temple servants, some dwelling in Jerusalem and others in Judah's cities. Chapter 11 names leaders such as Jedaiah, Jachin, and Seraiah, with their brothers counted and Zabdiel overseeing. Chapter 12 lists those who returned with Zerubbabel and Jeshua. At the dedication they purified themselves, the people, gates, and wall, and sounded trumpets while Judah rejoiced.

l: book of the genealogy, The Book of Nehemiah
s: records returning exiles [those who came up at the first] The narrator finds this book of the genealogy of those who came up at the first, and the chapter copies its contents. It lists the returnees by family and town, along with priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, temple servants, and Solomon's servants, and gives a total count.

l: Israel, The Book of Nehemiah
s: Israel is the covenant people whose story is traced from exile to renewed commitment. Carried away by Nebuchadnezzar, the returnees go back to Judah and Jerusalem, each to his own city, totaling 42,360 plus 7,337 servants and 245 singers, and they settle in their cities. A retrospective recalls how the fathers, rescued from Egypt and sustained in the wilderness, hardened their necks, made a molded calf, killed prophets, and ignored the commandments, yet the LORD did not forsake them. The people then swear an oath, with chiefs sealing it, to keep marriage restrictions, the Sabbath and seventh year, offerings, first fruits, and tithes, and not to forsake God's house. Finally, on hearing the law, Israel separates the mixed multitude from itself, and Nehemiah warns against profaning the Sabbath, recalling how Solomon was led to sin by foreign women.

l: temple servants, The Book of Nehemiah
s: Temple servants, listed by family names from Ziha through Hatipha, total 392 with Solomon's servants' children, and live in Ophel and their cities among Israel.

l: unregistered families, The Book of Nehemiah
s: Unregistered families came up from Tel Melah, Tel Harsha, Cherub, Addon and Immer but could not prove by fathers' houses or offspring whether they were Israelites; the children of Delaiah, Tobiah and Nekoda numbered 642.

l: disqualified priests, The Book of Nehemiah
s: Descendants of Hobaiah, Hakkoz, and Barzillai, priestly families, searched for genealogical records but found none. Deemed disqualified, they were removed from the priesthood, and the governor forbade them the most holy things until a priest ministered with Urim and Thummim.

l: gifts for the work, The Book of Nehemiah
s: A record of contributions to the treasury for the work. The governor gave 1,000 darics of gold, 50 basins and 530 priests' garments; heads of fathers' households gave 20,000 darics and 2,200 minas of silver; the rest of the people gave 20,000 darics, 2,000 minas of silver and 67 garments.

l: genealogical registration of the returnees, The Book of Nehemiah
s: was_prompted_by God [put into Nehemiah's heart] God puts it in the narrator's heart to gather the people to be listed by genealogy, and he uses the found genealogy book as the basis. Registration determines status: families who could not prove their lineage were set aside, and priests without records were removed from the priesthood.

l: Ezra, The Book of Nehemiah
s: Ezra is a scribe and priest who publicly reads the law before the assembly from a wooden pulpit, blessing the LORD, then meets household heads, priests, and Levites to study it, continuing daily readings through the feast.

l: Levites, The Book of Nehemiah
s: The Levites are a group of temple servants and teachers in Israel who appear throughout the records as religious leaders, singers, and recipients of sacred provisions. Named leaders such as Jeshua, Bani, Kadmiel, and Sherebiah recur. Early on they teach the people the law, reading distinctly and giving the sense, and calming the people on the holy day. They then lead the assembly in crying out, confession, and long prayer, and join the princes and priests in sealing the covenant. The covenant establishes their support: they receive tithes of the ground in farming villages and must bring the tithe of the tithes to the treasure house in the house of God. Later 284 Levites live in Jerusalem, under leaders including Uzzi of the sons of Asaph, while other divisions settle in Judah's cities and Benjamin's territory. Singers have settled provision by the king's commandment. Chiefs praise according to David's commandment, serve as gatekeepers at storehouses, are summoned for the dedication, purify themselves and the people, and set apart portions for Aaron's sons. The account ends with a lapse: the Levites and singers fled to their fields because portions were unpaid. Nehemiah gathers them back, appoints faithful treasurers, and restores their appointed duties.

l: book of the law of Moses, The Book of Nehemiah
s: The book of the law of Moses, commanded by the LORD to Israel and attributed to Moses. At the people's request Ezra brought it and it was read publicly; leaders found the booths command and read it daily through the feast.

l: wide place in front of the water gate, The Book of Nehemiah
s: hosts temporary shelters (booths) [built there during the feast] This was the open space where all the people gathered and where Ezra read the law from early morning until midday. It was also one of the places where people later built temporary shelters.

l: God's house, The Book of Nehemiah
s: has_part rooms [where the vessels of the sanctuary are kept] The house of God is the focus of the covenant's financial and ritual provisions: the yearly third-shekel charge supports its service, including the show bread, offerings, Sabbaths, feasts, and sin offerings. Wood, first fruits, firstborn, and tithes are brought to it, with rooms and a treasure house storing them. The chapter closes with the vow, 'We will not forsake the house of our God.'

l: public reading of the law, The Book of Nehemiah
s: A public reading of the law led by Ezra on the first day of the seventh month in the wide place before the water gate; Levites explained it, the people wept, then celebrated understanding, and reading continued daily through the feast.

l: Feast of Booths, The Book of Nehemiah
s: The Feast of Booths is a seven-day festival in the seventh month, commanded by the LORD through Moses, requiring Israelites to dwell in temporary booths. Leaders found the command in the law, proclaimed it, and the people kept it with an eighth-day solemn assembly and great gladness.

l: temporary shelters (booths), The Book of Nehemiah
s: made_of tree branches [olive, wild olive, myrtle, palm, thick trees] The people gathered olive, wild olive, myrtle, palm, and other thick-tree branches to make temporary shelters. They built them on rooftops, in courts, in the courts of God's house, and in the wide places of the water gate and Ephraim's gate, and the returned exiles lived in them.

l: Abraham, The Book of Nehemiah
s: Abraham, formerly Abram, is chosen by the LORD and brought out of Ur of the Chaldees, renamed, found faithful in heart, and given a covenant promising his offspring the land of six named peoples.

l: Sabbath, The Book of Nehemiah
s: Nehemiah saw Judeans working and merchants selling on the Sabbath, and rebuked the nobles for profaning it. He had the gates shut at dusk before the Sabbath and kept closed until it ended, posted his servants there, and later had the Levites guard the gates to sanctify the day.

l: land of Canaan, The Book of Nehemiah
s: Land of Canaan was inhabited by Canaanites, promised to Abraham's offspring, and possessed when the LORD subdued them. It held fortified cities, houses, cisterns, vineyards, olive groves and fruit trees; now its abundant yield goes to kings because of Israel's sins.

l: sure covenant, The Book of Nehemiah
s: is_sealed_by Levites [along with princes and priests] The people declare at the end of the prayer that they make a sure covenant and write it. Their princes, Levites, and priests seal it. It is their response to the confession of their sins and of the LORD's justice.

l: assembly with fasting and confession, The Book of Nehemiah
s: A communal gathering on the twenty-fourth day of the month: people in sackcloth and dirt, separated from foreigners, read the law for a fourth of the day, then confess and worship for another fourth, after which Levites lead a prayer recounting the LORD's works and the people's failures.

l: priests, The Book of Nehemiah
s: The priests are a group of twenty-one named sealers of the covenant, including Seraiah, who swear its oath and curse. They are to receive first fruits, wave offerings, new wine and oil at the house of God's rooms, and a descendant of Aaron attends the Levites during tithes.

l: peoples of the lands, The Book of Nehemiah
s: The peoples of the lands are those from whom the covenanting people had separated themselves to follow the law of God. The people vow not to give their daughters to them or take their daughters for their sons. They also vow not to buy wares or grain from them on the Sabbath or a holy day.

l: oath and curse (covenant), The Book of Nehemiah
s: A covenant sworn by the people, with their brothers and nobles, under oath and curse to walk in God's law and keep all the LORD's commandments, ordinances, and statutes. Its terms forbid intermarriage with the peoples of the land and buying on the Sabbath or holy days, require forgoing seventh year crops and debt exaction, and commit them to a yearly temple tax, wood offering, and bringing firstborn sons, livestock, and tithes. Leaders sealed it by name.

l: law of God, The Book of Nehemiah
s: given_through Moses [servant of God] The law of God was given by Moses the servant of God, and the people bind themselves by oath to walk in it. It is cited as the basis for the wood offering and for the firstborn of sons, livestock, herds, and flocks being brought to the house of God.

l: first fruits and tithes, The Book of Nehemiah
s: delivered_to house of God [yearly first fruits of ground and trees] The people pledge to bring the first fruits of the ground and of all kinds of trees, the firstborn of sons and livestock, and the first fruits of dough, wave offerings, new wine, and oil to the priests at the house of God. The tithes of the ground go to the Levites in the farming villages, and the Levites bring the tithe of the tithes to the treasure house. The offerings are brought to the rooms where the vessels of the sanctuary are.

l: princes of the people, The Book of Nehemiah
s: lives_in Jerusalem The princes of the people lived in Jerusalem.

l: people (people of the province), The Book of Nehemiah
s: The people of the province cast lots so one in ten would live in Jerusalem while nine parts stayed in other cities, and they blessed the men who willingly volunteered to dwell there.

l: cities of Judah, The Book of Nehemiah
s: In the cities of Judah, everyone lived on his own possession: Israel, the priests, the Levites, the temple servants, and the children of Solomon's servants. The residue of Israel, the priests, and the Levites lived there, each in his inheritance.

l: children of Benjamin, The Book of Nehemiah
s: The children of Benjamin settled in two areas: some in Jerusalem, led by Sallu with 928 men under overseer Joel and second-in-command Judah; others from Geba onward in Michmash, Bethel, Anathoth, Nob, Lod, and Ono.

l: lots casting, The Book of Nehemiah
s: sends_one_of_ten_to Jerusalem [nine parts live in the other cities] The people cast lots to determine which one of every ten would dwell in Jerusalem, the holy city. The other nine parts lived in the other cities.

l: dedication of the wall of Jerusalem, The Book of Nehemiah
s: The dedication of Jerusalem's wall was a joyful celebration with thanksgiving and music. Levites and singers were gathered to Jerusalem; priests, Levites, people, gates and wall were purified, then processions, great sacrifices and rejoicing followed, and men were appointed over storerooms.

l: two thanksgiving companies, The Book of Nehemiah
s: Nehemiah appointed two great thanksgiving companies to process on the wall: one led by Hoshaiah with princes, trumpeting priests and Ezra toward the dung gate, the other with Nehemiah and half the people meeting them; both ended standing in God's house.

l: room (Tobiah's room in the temple courts), The Book of Nehemiah
s: The great room had previously stored the meal offerings, frankincense, vessels and tithes of grain, new wine and oil, but Eliashib prepared it for Tobiah. Nehemiah had Tobiah's goods thrown out, the rooms cleansed, and the vessels, meal offerings and frankincense brought back in.

l: Jews who married foreign women, The Book of Nehemiah
s: married_women_of Ashdod [also Ammon and Moab] Nehemiah saw Jews who had married women of Ashdod, Ammon and Moab, whose children spoke half in the speech of Ashdod and not the Jews' language. He contended with them, cursed them, struck some, plucked out their hair, and made them swear not to intermarry. One son of Joiada, son-in-law to Sanballat, was chased away.

l: intermarriage, The Book of Nehemiah
s: Marriage with foreign women is treated as great evil and trespass against God, and Nehemiah cites Solomon, who was caused to sin by foreign women. He made the offenders swear not to give or take daughters in marriage with foreigners, and said such marriages defiled the priesthood and its covenant.

l: Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: This document is the book of Ecclesiastes, twelve chapters of reflection by the Preacher, son of David and king in Jerusalem, on what a person gains from life under the sun. Its central figures are the Preacher and God, who gives, judges and sets the limits of human understanding. Its recurring refrain is that all is vanity, a chasing after wind. Chapter 1 opens with the Preacher's declaration of vanity, the endless cycles of nature, and the claim that nothing is new. He finds that great wisdom brings grief. In chapter 2 he tests pleasure and great building works, finds them empty, and sees that the wise and the fool share one fate. He despairs of leaving his labor to a successor, yet says that enjoying one's labor is from God's hand. Chapter 3 gives the catalogue of times for every activity, says God set eternity in human hearts, and recommends rejoicing and doing good. It notes that people share the fate of animals. Chapters 4 to 6 look at oppression, envy, solitary toil, the strength of companions, and the fleeting fame of rulers. They counsel few words before God and prompt payment of vows, and they warn that wealth never satisfies and may go unenjoyed, leaving a stillborn child arguably better off. Chapters 7 to 10 gather proverbs that favor wisdom over folly, patience over anger, and mourning over feasting. They advise against being overly righteous or wicked, and note that no one is free of sin. The Preacher says he found wisdom out of reach and God's work hidden, and that God made mankind upright but people seek many inventions. They urge obedience to the king, observe that justice is delayed and the righteous and wicked sometimes receive each other's due, and affirm that the fear of God will be rewarded. Death comes alike to all, the living have hope, and the dead know nothing. Time and chance happen to everyone, wisdom is better than strength, and a little folly spoils much. Chapter 11 urges generosity, diligent sowing despite uncertainty, and rejoicing in youth with judgment in mind. Chapter 12 ends by urging the reader to remember the Creator in youth before old age and death, pictured in vivid imagery, when the spirit returns to God. It repeats that all is vanity, praises the Preacher's teaching, and concludes that the whole duty of man is to fear God and keep his commandments, since God will judge every work.

l: the Preacher, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: The Preacher is a king in Jerusalem, the son of David, who rules Israel and claims great wisdom above all who preceded him there. The records present him as a reflective, teaching figure who tests life under the sun and repeatedly judges it vanity, a chasing after wind. In the opening chapter he introduces himself, applies his heart to seek out all that is done under the sky, and finds even the pursuit of wisdom, madness and folly to be a chasing after wind. In the second chapter he tests mirth, builds great works, amasses wealth and withholds no joy from himself, yet finds no profit. He hates his life and labor because death comes to the wise and the fool alike and he must leave his work to a successor, and he slides into despair. He then sees that eating, drinking and enjoying good in labor come from God's hand. In the third chapter he asks what profit labor brings, observes wickedness in the place of justice, says God will judge and tests people to show they are like animals, and concludes nothing is better than rejoicing in one's works. In the seventh chapter he says he tested everything by wisdom and resolved to be wise, but wisdom remained far from him. He found one man among a thousand but no woman, and concludes that God made mankind upright but people seek many inventions. In the eighth chapter he commends mirth, calls certain outcomes vanity, and concludes that the work of God cannot be found out. In the ninth chapter he finds that one event comes to all, that time and chance govern outcomes, and that wisdom is better than strength. In the final chapter he declares 'Vanity of vanities! All is vanity!' and is described as wise, still teaching the people knowledge, and setting in order many proverbs while seeking acceptable words of truth written blamelessly. He moves from search and despair toward enjoyment, humility before God, and teaching.

l: God, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: God appears in these records as the sovereign Creator and giver, portrayed across the chapters as the one who stands behind human life, labor, fortune, and judgment. He dwells in heaven while people are on earth, so words before him should be few, and he takes no pleasure in fools who delay their vows. He is named as Creator who made mankind upright, gave the spirit that returns to him at death, and gave people their days under the sun. The record opens with God as source of enjoyment in eating, drinking, and labor. He gives wisdom, knowledge, and joy to the one who pleases him, while the sinner receives the travail of gathering and heaping up, which passes to the one who pleases God. He gives people a heavy burden, yet makes everything beautiful in its time and sets eternity in their hearts, though they cannot find out his work from beginning to end. His works last forever, with nothing added or taken away, so that people fear him. He judges righteous and wicked and tests people to show they are like animals. Later chapters stress his gifts and his control. He gives life, riches, wealth, and the power to enjoy them as his gift, but may give a man riches and withhold the power to eat them, so an alien eats instead. He is mightier than man, who cannot contend with him. He makes prosperity and adversity side by side, and no one can straighten what he has made crooked. Those who fear him fare better, and the wicked do not. The righteous and wise and their works are in his hand, though man cannot know whether love or hatred awaits him, and he has accepted the works of one who enjoys bread and wine. He does all, and his work is unknowable. The account ends in judgment: he will bring the young man into judgment for his ways, and finally every work, including every hidden thing, whether good or evil. The reader is told to remember the Creator in youth and to fear him.

l: vanity, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: Vanity is the central theme of the Preacher's verdict in Ecclesiastes, summed up as 'Vanity of vanities, all is vanity,' and equated with a chasing after wind. It characterizes all things, all that comes, and all human and animal fate. The records trace it from beginning to end. Chapter 1 declares it over all works under the sun, including the pursuit of wisdom, madness and folly. Chapter 2 applies it to mirth, great works, the lack of profit, the shared fate of wise and fool, and labor left to a successor who did not work for it, called a great evil. Chapter 3 applies it to man's lack of advantage over animals, who share one breath and fate, after noting wickedness in places of justice. Chapter 4 ties it to envy-driven labor, the solitary man's endless toil, and a popular young king's fading succession. Chapter 6 links it to unenjoyed riches, the stillborn child, the wandering of desire, and the many words that multiply it. Chapter 11 extends it to youth and the dawn of life, and chapter 12 restates the verdict after the description of aging and death.

l: human labor, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: Human labor is portrayed as yielding no clear gain under the sun. It begins with a rhetorical question about what man gains, then calls labor and the search for understanding a heavy burden God gave humanity to be afflicted with, and ends by declaring all works vanity and chasing after wind.

l: sons of men, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: The sons of men are portrayed as mortal creatures made from dust who share the animals' fate of death and hold no advantage over them. God tests them to show this. They bear heavy misery, lack power over the spirit and knowledge of the future, and cannot fully discover God's work however much they labor, though eternity is set in their hearts. Their hearts lean toward evil because sentence is delayed. The records move from this burden and limitation to the repeated counsel to rejoice, do good, eat, drink, and enjoy labor.

l: nothing new, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: The principle from Ecclesiastes 1 that nothing is new under the sun: what has been will be again. The Preacher asks whether anything is new, answers that it already existed in earlier ages, and notes that former and later things go unremembered by those who follow.

l: wisdom, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: Wisdom is a topic in Ecclesiastes, presented with tension. The Preacher first recounts seeking it in Chapter 1, gaining great wisdom, yet finding that it is a chasing after wind and that more wisdom and knowledge bring more grief and sorrow. Chapter 7 praises it as good as an inheritance, a defense like money, a preserver of its owner's life, and a strength greater than ten rulers, though it felt far from him. Chapter 9 ranks it better than strength and weapons of war, but notes the poor man's wisdom is despised and one sinner can destroy much good.

l: wisdom, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: Wisdom is a topic in Chapter 2: it excels folly as light excels darkness and stays with the narrator, yet the wise and the fool share one fate and are forgotten, so he calls it vanity; God gives wisdom to those pleasing him.

l: fool (the foolish), Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: The fool is a recurring figure of folly who walks in darkness and does evil without knowing it. Early on, wisdom excels folly, yet the fool shares the wise man's fate of being forgotten, and the narrator fears a fool may succeed him. Later, the fool's many words resemble a dream with many cares, and God takes no pleasure in fools who delay vows. Finally, their hearts dwell in the house of mirth, anger rests in their bosom, and their song is worse than the wise man's rebuke.

l: mirth and pleasure, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: Mirth and pleasure is a theme the narrator weighs. In Chapter 2 he tests himself with wine and joy, calls laughter foolishness, and judges the pursuit vanity, yet allows enjoyment of labor is good from God's hand. In Chapter 8 he commends mirth: eating, drinking, and joy accompany labor all life's days.

l: great works and possessions (the narrator's), Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: The narrator's great works and possessions: houses, vineyards, gardens, pools, servants, herds, silver, gold, singers and instruments, surpassing all before him in Jerusalem. Reviewing them, he finds everything vanity with no profit under the sun, and hates his labor because he must leave it to his successor.

l: successor (the man who comes after the narrator), Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: The successor is the man who will come after the narrator and rule over all his labor, though whether he will be wise or a fool is unknown. The narrator laments that labor may pass to one who did not earn it, calling this vanity and a great evil.

l: death, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: Death is the one event that befalls everyone alike: wise and fool, righteous and wicked, people and animals. It is an appointed time, returning all to dust. It erases memory, so wisdom confers no lasting advantage, feeding the narrator's hatred of life and despair over labor he must leave behind. After it, all go to Sheol, where there is no work, plan, knowledge or wisdom.

l: animals, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: Animals share the fate of the sons of men: they die as people die, have one breath, and come from and return to dust, while the narrator questions whether their spirit goes downward.

l: time and seasons, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: applies_to every purpose under heaven The chapter opens by declaring a season and a time for every purpose under heaven, then lists paired opposites such as birth and death, planting and plucking up, and war and peace. God has made everything beautiful in its time, and there is a time for every purpose and work in judgment.

l: enjoyment of life as God’s gift, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: Enjoyment of life is presented as God's gift: eating, drinking, rejoicing, and enjoying the good of one's labor. It is called a person's proper portion, especially since no one can see what comes after him. First, the narrator questions labor's profit yet affirms rejoicing and doing good. Later, the power to enjoy riches and labor is God's gift, keeping the person joyfully occupied so he seldom broods over life's days.

l: the oppressed, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: has_state no comforter The oppressed are seen weeping under the sun with no comforter. Their plight leads the speaker to praise the dead and the unborn above the living.

l: oppressors, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: Oppressors are a group who hold power on their side and oppress the oppressed, who consequently have no comforter, as Chapter 4 describes.
